source.title: Lukas (2026), Waving Through Ontogeny: The Larval Chondrocranial Development of Staurois parvus
source.version: International Journal of Zoology 2026, Article 8862952; version of record first published 2026-03-31
source.locator: Results §3.1 (observation at 27Go); Discussion §4.1 (absence of larval otic process and need for further taxonomic investigation); Methods §§2.1–2.2 (116 larvae, stages 19–27, Vienna Zoo Schönbrunn breeding facility)

source.scope: Larval chondrocranial description and developmental observations from 116 larvae spanning Gosner stages 19–27; the article describes stage 27 morphology. Larvae were provided by the Vienna Zoo Schönbrunn breeding facility. Sample collection dates are not reported.
source.rightsHolder: Paul Lukas (2026); article copyright notice applies under the Creative Commons Attribution License.
source.licenseAppliesTo: Article text and content under its Creative Commons Attribution License; third-party material separately credited is excluded. This dossier paraphrases article text and does not reuse figures.
source.attribution: Lukas P (2026). Waving Through Ontogeny: The Larval Chondrocranial Development of Staurois parvus. International Journal of Zoology 2026:8862952. https://doi.org/10.1155/ijz/8862952. Claims paraphrased.

claim.text: In the described larval chondrocranium at Gosner stage 27, Staurois parvus lacked a larval otic process; the author identifies this as a possible distinguishing feature whose taxonomic level needs investigation in other ranids.
claim.placeTimeScope: Vienna Zoo Schönbrunn breeding facility, Austria; one developmental series of 116 larvae across Gosner stages 19–27, including 11 stage-27 larvae. Article first published 2026-03-31; sample collection dates are not stated.
claim.lifeStatus: Larvae were provided by a zoo breeding facility. This is captive-facility material and does not describe wild-collected larvae or population-level variation.

gaps: The developmental series is from one breeding facility; it does not establish variation among wild populations, species-wide prevalence, or the taxonomic diagnostic value of the observed feature.
